title: transition from swifterbant to funnelbeaker: a bayesian chronological model
display_name: Transition from Swifterbant to Funnelbeaker: A Bayesian Chronological Model
abstract: abstract the transition from the late swifterbant culture to the first appearance of the funnelbeaker westgroup raises numerous questions, from cultural discontinuities to gradual transitions. this process describes the transformation from a late mesolithic of hunter gatherer societies to a fully neolithic society in northwestern europe. the early neolithic in this area marks a technological and sociocultural transition zone, which we can identify. although the first megalithic buildings of the funnelbeaker culture were erected around 3600 bc, swifterbant sites and findings can still be traced. many studies assume a hiatus between these phases, which is based on a research historical but also a conservation related problem. with this contribution, we attempt to generate a chronological bayesian model on the basis of absolute chronological data. the aim is to compare the numerous available radiocarbon data from different periods in one overview. it is a model to visualize discontinuities or overlaps of the currently available data. it becomes apparent that there is a slide overlap between the archaeologically defined chronological phases. this model serves as a basis for further discussion and chronological models.
classification_path: Humanity and Art > History and Archaeology > Archaeology > Historical Archaeology

title: traditional flat breads spread from the fertile crescent: production process and history of baking systems
display_name: Traditional flat breads spread from the Fertile Crescent: Production process and history of baking systems
abstract: thef lat breads include a multitude of bread types different from each other but are always relatively thin, ranging from a few millimeters to a few centimeters in thickness. these breads, whose origin is very ancient, fit well into the context of a subsistence economy: i) they can be obtained from cereals other than wheat, such as pseudocereals or legumes, allowing the use of sustainable local productions from marginal lands; ii) they do not necessarily require an oven to be baked; iii) they can serve as a dish and as a spoon/fork; iv) they can be dehydrated by a second baking process, preventing the growth of molds and extending the shelf life; v) they are transported with little encumbrance. these strong points make flat breads very popular, traditionally in near east and central asia and also in some mediterranean areas, in the arabian peninsula, and in the indian subcontinent. by a multidisciplinary approach, this review gives an insight into the variety of traditional flat breads from the fertile crescent and related regions, classifying them on the basis of their production process. moreover, the baking systems adopted to prepare flat breads are reviewed, such as vertical ovens (tannur and tabun) and griddles (saj), whose structure, origin, history, and values are described in detail. this overview shows that these breads have survived until today because of their versatility. in fact, flat breads can be produced both in the same way as they were made thousands of years ago and in modern fully automatic industrial lines, allowing tradition to meet innovation.

title: the nooscope manifested: ai as instrument of knowledge extractivism
display_name: The Nooscope manifested: AI as instrument of knowledge extractivism
abstract: abstract some enlightenment regarding the project to mechanise reason. the assembly line of machine learning: data, algorithm, model. the training dataset: the social origins of machine intelligence. the history of ai as the automation of perception. the learning algorithm: compressing the world into a statistical model. all models are wrong, but some are useful. world to vector: the society of classification and prediction bots. faults of a statistical instrument: the undetection of the new. adversarial intelligence vs. statistical intelligence: labour in the age of ai.

title: rolling out revolution: using radiocarbon dating in archaeology
display_name: Rolling Out Revolution: Using Radiocarbon Dating in Archaeology
abstract: sixty years ago, the advent of radiocarbon dating rewrote archaeological chronologies around the world. forty years ago, the advent of calibration signaled the death knell of the diffusionism that had been the mainstay of archaeological thought for a century. since then, the revolution has continued, as the extent of calibration has been extended ever further back and as the range of material that can be dated has been expanded. now a new revolution beckons, one that could allow archaeology to engage in historical debate and usher in an entirely new kind of (pre)history. this paper focuses on more than a decade of experience in utilizing bayesian approaches routinely for the interpretation of 14 c dates in english archaeology, discussing both the practicalities of implementing these methods and their potential for changing archaeological thinking.
classification_path: Humanity and Art > History and Archaeology > Archaeology > Historical Archaeology

title: advances in the household archaeology of highland mesoamerica
display_name: Advances in the Household Archaeology of Highland Mesoamerica
abstract: recent investigations and reconsideration of households in the mesoamerican highlands illustrate the central role of domestic spheres of interaction to the broader cultural dynamics of the region over four millennia. methodological advances in the analysis of past houses permit more sophisticated social reconstructions of the spaces and activities that constituted domestic life for the diverse peoples of the region. current studies highlight the economic interdependence and diversification of households, their strategic flexibility in affiliation, the integrative ritual practices undertaken within domestic spaces, the material correlates of prestige competition between households, and the manner in which households articulated with a larger social universe.
classification_path: Humanity and Art > History and Archaeology > Archaeology > Historical Archaeology

title: palaeoecological, archaeological and historical data and the making of d evon landscapes. i . t he b lackdown h ills
display_name: Palaeoecological, archaeological and historical data and the making of<scp>D</scp>evon landscapes.<scp>I</scp>.<scp>T</scp>he<scp>B</scp>lackdown<scp>H</scp>ills
abstract: this paper presents the first systematic study of the vegetation history of a range of low hills in sw e ngland, uk, lying between more researched fenlands and uplands. after the palaeoecological sites were located bespoke archaeological, historical and documentary studies of the surrounding landscape were undertaken specifically to inform palynological interpretation at each site. the region has a distinctive archaeology with late m esolithic tool scatters, some evidence of early n eolithic agriculture, many b ronze a ge funerary monuments and r omano b ritish iron working. historical studies have suggested that the present landscape pattern is largely early m edieval. however, the pollen evidence suggests a significantly different h olocene vegetation history in comparison with other areas in lowland e ngland, with evidence of incomplete forest clearance in later p rehistory ( b ronze i ron a ge). woodland persistence on steep, but poorly drained, slopes, was probably due to the unsuitability of these areas for mixed farming. instead they may have been under woodland management (e.g. coppicing) associated with the iron working industry. data from two of the sites also suggest that later i ron a ge and r omano b ritish impact may have been geographically restricted. the documented m edieval land management that maintained the patchwork of small fields, woods and heathlands had its origins in later p rehistory, but there is also evidence of landscape change in the 6th 9th centuries ad . we conclude that the b lackdown h ills area was one of many distinctive subregions , which due to a combination of edaphic, topographic and cultural factors could qualify as an eco cultural region or pays . it is argued that the use of such eco culturally distinctive regions or pays can provide a spatial and archaeological framework for palaeoecology, which has implications for landscape research, designation and heritage management.
classification_path: Humanity and Art > History and Archaeology > Archaeology > Historical Archaeology

title: modern human origins and the evolution of behavior in the later pleistocene record of south asia
display_name: Modern Human Origins and the Evolution of Behavior in the Later Pleistocene Record of South Asia
abstract: the archaeological record of later pleistocene south asia has a crucial role to play in our understanding of the evolution of modern human behavior and the dispersal of anatomically modern humans around the old world. later pleistocene records of south asia are here summarized and placed in the context of the modernhumanorigins debate. aspects of the south asian record share familiar traits with other regions of the old world, but south asia also appears to have its own adaptive features and material culture developments. the fluctuating environment during the later pleistocene would have influenced the adaptations of anatomically modern and archaic humans, affecting population size, movement, and the usefulness of cultural innovations. on the basis of prevailing genetic, archaeological, and biogeographic information, it is hypothesized that homo sapiens colonized south asia as part of an early southern dispersal from africa. the effect of demographic processes on the rate and direction of cultural change is proposed as an explanation for the lack of a symbolic revolution signaling the arrival of anatomically modern humans on the indian subcontinent. instead, the late paleolithic represents a diversification of adaptive behaviors that may be traced to the middle paleolithic.
classification_path: Humanity and Art > History and Archaeology > Archaeology > Historical Archaeology

title: evolving museum identities and paradoxical response strategies to identity challenges and ambiguities
display_name: Evolving Museum Identities and Paradoxical Response Strategies to Identity Challenges and Ambiguities
abstract: there has been little research into how organizations modify their identities in response to the various ethical and cultural changes that occur in wider society. this qualitative investigation of recent museum approaches to handling human remains is situated within a critique of museum identity dynamics in history, archaeological, and science museums in the u.k. public sector. the theoretical framework encapsulates various paradoxes inherent in museum response strategies to such identity challenges. this study reveals the discursive practices museums use to legitimate and privilege their historical identities, while simultaneously engaging with different alternative identities in processes defined here as organizational sensitivization. these involve either amalgamating identity challenges or diffusing them, usually by means of open dialogue. those challenges perceived to be identity threats are marginalized by the museums to protect their articulated identities through engagement in self-legitimization processes. this can leave museums with paradoxically unresolved tensions and identity ambiguities.
classification_path: Humanity and Art > History and Archaeology > Archaeology > Historical Archaeology

title: war in the southwest, war in the world
display_name: War in the Southwest, War in the World
abstract: the study of warfare in the ancient pueblos of the u.s. southwest has become politicized and contentious, and southwestern data are only rarely used to address larger anthropological theories of war. a cross-cultural model of violence proposed by carol and melvin ember (1992) suggests that war in pre-state societies is predicted by resource unpredictability and socialization for fear. the ember and ember model is evaluated using syntheses of southwestern warfare by steven leblanc (1999), environmental variability by jeffrey dean (1988, 1996), and political history by stephen lekson (1999). the fit between the southwestern data and the model is close, and supports the ember and ember model.
classification_path: Humanity and Art > History and Archaeology > Archaeology > Historical Archaeology

title: vulnerability of worldwide pastoralism to global changes and interdisciplinary strategies for sustainable pastoralism
display_name: Vulnerability of Worldwide Pastoralism to Global Changes and Interdisciplinary Strategies for Sustainable Pastoralism
abstract: ten case studies from seven major pastoral regions across six continents were studied in this paper by conceptualizing three factors (agro-ecosystem resilience, livelihood options, and institution capacity) as the axes of a three-dimensional vulnerability framework. this analysis highlights the vulnerability of agriculture-based livelihood systems to global changes and helps identify what institutions have the potential to mobilize effective relief in different pastoral regions. in terms of results, this vulnerability assessment shows that the vulnerability of pastoralism was very different in all the cases across the globe. as such, a further analysis, based on the pressure-state-response (psr) model was undertaken to enhance our understanding of the ways that global changes put pressures on pastoral livelihoods worldwide. from this we conclude that climate change and climate variability are driving fragile pastoral ecosystems into more vulnerable conditions. socioeconomic factors, such as changes in land tenure, agriculture, sedentarization, and institutions are fracturing large-scale pastoral ecosystems into spatially isolated systems. the implications of this analysis are that professionals, practitioners, and policy makers should jointly develop a coupled human and natural systems approach that focuses on enhancing the resilience of pastoral communities and their practices. this requires institutional developments to support asset building and good governance to enhance adaptive capability. in addition, pastoralists' adaptation strategies to global change need to be supported by public awareness and improved by institutional decisions at different scales and dimensions.
classification_path: Humanity and Art > History and Archaeology > Archaeology > Historical Archaeology

title: epilogue: changing archaeological perspectives upon historical ecology in the pacific islands
display_name: Epilogue: Changing Archaeological Perspectives upon Historical Ecology in the Pacific Islands
abstract: late-twentieth-century archaeological perspectives upon historical ecology in the pacific islands emphasized anthropogenic impacts documented particularly in studies of vegetation change and deforestation, and the depletion or extinction of native faunas. more complex views of cultural-environmental relationships are now emerging. biological invasions are seen as occurring more variably than in the transported landscapes model, simplistic narratives of cultural collapse are shown as only partly in agreement with relevant data, and models of behavioral ecology are argued as insufficient to explain long-term trajectories of ecological change. more influential roles are being proposed for climatic and demographic factors and cultural agency in ecological relations.
classification_path: Humanity and Art > History and Archaeology > Archaeology > Historical Archaeology

title: scientific reviews: using neutron imaging methods for non-invasive investigation of museum objects
display_name: Scientific Reviews: Using Neutron Imaging Methods for Non-Invasive Investigation of Museum Objects
abstract: an important part of our cultural heritage can only be learned from the study of objects that have been preserved from ancient times. a small fraction of these objects are can be admired in museums because of their beauty or historical relevance. however, the majority of such objects are not exhibited and mainly used for scientific and archaeological investigations. the information we can extract from such samples provides important contributions to our knowledge about history, living conditions, and cultural activities. many of the objects are unique and can only be studied non-destructively in order to preserve them for future generations. conventional chemical methods are therefore excluded. title: historical linguistics in australia: trees, networks and their implications
display_name: Historical linguistics in Australia: trees, networks and their implications
abstract: this paper presents an overview of the current state of historical linguistics in australian languages. australian languages have been important in theoretical debates about the nature of language change and the possibilities for reconstruction and classification in areas of intensive diffusion. here are summarized the most important outstanding questions for australian linguistic prehistory; i also present a case study of the karnic subgroup of pama nyungan, which illustrates the problems for classification in australian languages and potential approaches using phylogenetic methods.
classification_path: Humanity and Art > History and Archaeology > Archaeology > Historical Archaeology

title: archaeology of cuisine and cooking
display_name: Archaeology of Cuisine and Cooking
abstract: this review demonstrates that recent contributions by archaeologists to the study of cuisine and cooking present a new addition to the field of anthropology. archaeologists situate their work historically and contextually by examining cuisines that are culturally constructed. studying cooking and food preparation helps elucidate relationships among material practices, understandings of taste, identity, power, and meaning in a society. archaeologists can not only discover specific ingredients in food, but also reconstruct recipes, decipher regional cuisines, ascertain sensory experiences, recover the tools in spatial context, recreate techniques used to prepare food in the past, and overall learn more about the social and cultural contexts of the human experience. this type of investigation is possible because archaeological work uses complementary data to explain social practices and because advances in archaeological methods make accessible previously undetectable data. experimental archaeology focused on cooking in the past has not only revealed important social information but also captured the imagination of the public. archaeological research on cooking and cuisine reveals social, political, religious, and economic practices in the past, and it has a unique ability to engage the present with the past through public outreach and solutions to food-related problems.
classification_path: Humanity and Art > History and Archaeology > Archaeology > Historical Archaeology

title: two ie phylogenies, three pie migrations, and four kinds of steppe pastoralism
display_name: Two IE phylogenies, three PIE migrations, and four kinds of steppe pastoralism
abstract: two ie phylogenies, three pie migrations, and four kinds of steppe pastoralismthis paper defends and elaborates a pontic-caspian steppe homeland for pie dated broadly between 4500-2500 bc.first i criticize the bouckaert et al. phylogeny, rooted in anatolia, published in science in august 2012.then i describe archaeological evidence for three migrations from the pontic-caspian steppes into neighboring regions, dated to 4500-2500 bc, that parallel the sequence and direction of movements for the first three branches in the ringe phylogeny (ringe, warnow and taylor 2002) of the indo-european languages: 1. anatolian, 2. tocharian, and 3. a complex split that separated italic, celtic, and perhaps germanic (germanic could be rooted in two places in their phylogeny).each of the migrations i described is suggested by purely archaeological evidence, unconnected with any hypothesis about language.they are dated about 4400-4200 bc for branch 1, 3300-2800 bc for 2, and 3000-2800 bc for 3.these three apparent prehistoric movements out of the pontic-caspian steppes match the directions expected for the first three splits in the ringe phylogeny, and the directions of later movements are plausible given the ringe sequence and the known later locations of the daughter branches.the parallel between the archaeological sequence and the linguistic sequence, each sequence derived from independent data, is argued to add archaeological plausibility to the hypothesis of the pontic-caspian homeland for pie.in addition, recent archaeological research on steppe economies and diets shows that it is misleading to regard "steppe pastoralism" as a single undifferentiated economic category.i suggest that we can link the three earliest periods of outward migration from the pontic-caspian steppes with particular kinds of pastoral economy in the steppes.i provided a brief characterization of four different kinds of steppe pastoralism relevant to indo-european migrations.

title: applications of raman spectroscopy in art and archaeology
display_name: Applications of Raman spectroscopy in art and archaeology
abstract: the 8th edition of the international congress on the application of raman spectroscopy in art archeology (raa 2015) was held in wroclaw (poland) from 1 to 5 september 2015, with three plenary lectures, eight trendsetting talks, 37 oral presentations and 34 poster presentations. the number of active participants was 113 delegates from 22 countries among the 250 authors that presented at least one work. the increasing importance of the application of raman spectroscopy in art and archaeology is illustrated by an increasing number of research papers published each year, and by the scientific conferences and sessions that have been dedicated to this research area in the past. in fact, raman spectroscopy is nowadays considered as the most adequate instrumental technique to identify and characterize the material component of the objects of art and antiquities. the biennial international congress on the application of raman spectroscopy in art and archaeology (raa) is probably the most important event dedicated to this topic. the raa conferences promote raman spectroscopy and play an important role in the increasing field of its application in art and archaeology. these prominent international events have a long tradition. previously they were held in london (2001),1 ghent (2003),2 paris (2005),3 modena (2007),4 bilbao (2009),5 parma (2011)6 and ljubljana (2013).7 the eighth edition of the international congress on the application of raman spectroscopy in art and archeology (raa 2015) was held in wroclaw (poland) from 1 to 5 september 2015. as in the previous editions, the scientific programme was focused on the characterization of materials, conservation issues affecting cultural heritage, raman spectroscopy of organic-based materials and raman applications in archaeology and forensics with authenticity research. these studies were presented along three plenary lectures, eight trendsetting talks, 37 oral presentations and 34 poster presentations. the number of active participants was 113 delegates from 22 countries among the 250 authors that presented at least one work to the congress. the high quality of the contributions is reflected in the selected 17 manuscripts covered in this special issue, ordered in topics suggested to participants when this raa2015 edition was announced. the most interesting aspects of such manuscripts are highlighted below. the spectral interpretation is not always an easy task. for example, in polymorphic discrimination or in the discrimination of natural and synthetic forms of certain pigments, especially if this discrimination is performed manually where the subjectivity of the researcher can introduce misinterpretations. a system to automatically classify the spectral data into specific and well-known classes, that is, references classes, is proposed in the work by gonzalez-vidal et al..8 the assignation procedure is based on a combination of chemometric techniques, providing a powerful way to achieve spectral separability and discrimination capability between very similar spectra, all performed in an automatic way. a decision-making algorithm was specifically developed to select the corresponding reference class with no user input, which was successfully validated using simulated spectra. the implemented classification system was applied on experimental raman spectra of pigments commonly present in artist's paints, providing reliable and consistent results. costantini et al.9 have demonstrated the usefulness of raman spectroscopy not only to identify the different compounds present in efflorescence deposits, but to perform their semi-quantification in terms of compounds concentrations (as %) of such salt deposits based on the use of (1) external calibration curves through standard and sample preparation of pressed pellets and (2) the palme software that extracts the quantitative information using a multivariate linear regression approach (mlr) using the whole raman spectrum and considering it as a linear combination of pure spectra of the identified compounds. both methods were used to quantify real efflorescence salts found in the walls and wall paintings of the san esteban church in ribera de valderejo (basque country, spain) where portable raman spectroscopy identified gypsum (caso4 2h2o) and niter (kno3) in the efflorescence salts on the calcite (caco3) mortar. the palme treatment was done on the raman spectra obtained in situ, while the external calibration required a previous sampling and the subsequent pellet preparation in the laboratory. this research shown that the method based on the treatment of raman spectra with palme allows to obtain in-situ semi-quantitative results, in a much shorter time (minutes in fact), being comparable in quality (accuracy and uncertainty) with those obtained using the external calibration curve method. raman spectra of a set of chrome logwood inks prepared in the laboratory according to a basic mid-19th century recipe were acquired by centeno et al.10 those spectra were the basis to understand that the vibrational features depend in part on the proportions of logwood extract to k2cro4 used. moreover, the hues also depend on other conditions of the basic procedure, such as on the temperature that the logwood decoction is heated at. the results exemplified the complexity of the composition of artistic and writing inks colored by organic and organometallic compounds, the challenges that their noninvasive identification in works of art and in historic documents present and the need for comprehensive raman spectral libraries including inks prepared following as close as possible recipes in multiple historic sources and using different raw materials. finally, the inks used by vincent van gogh in street in saintes-maries-de-la-mer were characterized using the raman spectra acquired in this work. green compounds of natural or synthetic origin are found in many research areas related to cultural heritage science. however, a detailed and comprehensive database of spectra and references of such kind of green compounds is still missing in the literature. the paper by coccato et al.11 provides both a literature review and downloadable raman spectra of such reference green materials especially valuable in scientific cultural heritage studies. practical aspects regarding the laser wavelength selection are also discussed with regards to the comparison to published reference spectra. the range of studied green materials is wide and encompasses cu, fe, cr and co compounds. the usefulness of the database is illustrated by analysing a cross section of a green zone of the early netherlandish panel painting ghent altarpiece by the van eyck brothers. opals are naturally occurring hydrous silica materials (sio2 nh2o), characterized by different degrees of crystallinity and crystal structure. because of their optical properties, opals have been largely used as decorative elements in artworks. sodo et al.12 have performed a systematic analysis by raman, ftir and xrd of nine opals sampled all around the world (australia, madagascar, slovakia, brazil, mexico, honduras and ethiopia). opals from ethiopia, honduras, brazil and mexico showed patterns typical of opal-ct, generally associated to volcanic genesis, while australia, madagascar and slovakia opals are opal-a type, associated to sedimentary origin. the presence of co2 was detected as homogeneously distributed (ftir imaging) only in the latter group, and exceptionally in the honduras sample. however, opals-ct are co2-free. the obtained results contribute to increase the database of the chemical physical properties of opals. micro-raman spectroscopy was used by ev k et al.13 to follow the carbonation reaction, up to 16 weeks, in lime paste produced with a traditional technology and cured under controlled conditions. moreover, authors visualized the transformation of calcium hydroxide into calcium carbonate using raman imaging. calcite was the only crystalline caco3 polymorph detected under the conditions of the experiment. three sharp zones of pure portlandite (ca(oh)2), partially carbonated portlandite and calcite (caco3), were distinguished from the spectroscopic image, being amorphous calcium carbonate the main compound within the carbonation front. the carbonation rate was found to be higher between first and second week of ageing, decreasing continuously until full carbonation was achieved after 16 weeks. portable raman spectroscopy was applied by garcia-florentino et al.14 to evaluate the original composition and possible deterioration products of the mortars used in the inner walls and those covering the concrete of the ceilings in a xx century monument, selecting the most appropriate sampling sites. in the laboratory, raman microscopy and raman imaging, assisted with sem-eds, xrd and ed-xrf imaging, allowed to identify the key compounds to understand the deterioration processes taking place in the mortars. the main pathologies identified in these mortars were two: (1) the first one belongs to the dehydration/hydration process of the original gypsum (caso4 2h2o) from the mortar and (2) the formation of efflorescence salts (reprecipitated calcite and gypsum, together with thenardite (na2so4), natron (na2co3 10 h2o), niter (kno3) and nitratine (nano3) as the main decaying salts) on and behind the mortars from the walls. an unusual black patina covering both the exterior and interior walls of the neang khmau temple, located in the archaeological khmer complex (cambodia), has been observed during a recent conservative survey. the monument was built by using laterite bricks (containing oxides of iron, aluminium, titanium and manganese), a natural material common in tropical areas as a weathering product of pre-existing rocks. the black patina is present in the four facades covering a relevant part of the vertical surfaces protected from rainfall and is also homogeneously distributed on the interior of the monument. casanova municchia et al.15 studied the mineralogical and chemical composition of the patina using a multianalytical approach to characterize the alteration products. analyses performed both on single fragments and on polished cross sections collected from all four temple facades and from one area in the temple interior showed the systematic presence of manganese mineral phases: hollandite (ba(mn4+6mn3+2)o16), romanechite ((ba,h2o)2(mn+4,mn+3)5o10) and manganite (mno(oh)). these black neominerals are precipitated in the surface of non-leachable areas of the monument from dissolved mn(ii), naturally leached from the laterite bricks during the variations of wet and dry seasons and transported by rainfall to the protected areas of the facades. micro-raman spectroscopy, complemented with sem and xrd, was used by marsza ek16 to identify the salts that crystallized within and on the weathered limestone and sandstone architectonic details of the blessed salomea sculpture and its arch in the cloister of the poor clares in krak w (poland). the limestone sculpture reveals the presence of black crusts containing gypsum (caso4 2h20) and barite (baso4); the white efflorescence salts of sandstones in the arch consist of thenardite (na2so4) and syngenite (k2ca(so4)2 h2o) while the salts in the sandstone pores revealed the presence of aphthitalite ((k,na)3na(so4)2), niter (kno3), nitratine (nano3) and burkeite (na4so4(co3)x(so4)1 x). these deterioration products have been mainly assigned to the impact of air pollution (so2 and nox) on the original materials and migration of dissolved ions from structural elements of the arch in the case of the sandstone. this characterization of the salts present in deteriorated stones helps in selecting the methods of stone desalination and conservation. some ottoman low carbon steel nails from a 16th century brick masonry dome of kili ali pasha bath (istanbul) and from a 19th century stone dwelling in phocaea (izmir) were studied by yucel et al.17 for their long-term corrosion characteristics using raman and sem/eds microscopic techniques. powdered samples scraped from the corrosion layers were studied also by xrd and ftir. the non correlation between xrd peak intensity and the abundance of oxides and oxihydroxides in the corrosion layer suggested the presence of amorphous phases the protective ability index (pai), expressed as the ratio of isotropic goethite raman band and the sum of raman bands because of magnetite (fe3o4), maghemite ( -fe2o3), hematite ( -fe2o3) and lepidocrocite ( -feo(oh), was used to characterize the state of the different corrosion layers of samples. corrosion mechanisms and pai values were concluded to be affected by compositional characteristics of artifacts and their atmospheric conditions. polyether-based polyurethane (pur) flexible foam has been used in many modern artworks. these pur materials have an expected life of 20 50 years; thus, an adequate preservation procedure is required to enlarge the live of pur-based artworks. de s et al.18 performed a natural ageing test on unaged (model pur) and naturally pre-aged (commercial pur) references, always in the dark and during 12 months at 45 55% relative humidity, comparing four storage conditions. the samples were analysed every 3 months by vis-nir, ftir and raman spectroscopic techniques. anova was used as the data treatment to identify significant spectral variations and to uncover correlations between molecular spectral lines and physical aspects. raman spectroscopy was the most adequate technique to detect the early stage pur molecular deterioration. for both model and commercial samples, open-air storage proved to be the most harmful condition, while anoxic storage showed the best results. the elucidation of the chemical composition of 16 early synthetic organic pigment powders from the lefranc experimental laboratory collection dating 1890 1914 was performed by gabrieli et al..19 it can be hypothesized that the most successful of these formulations could have been finalized in paint tubes and released onto the market, meaning that they may even be found in artworks from the same period. the availability of the lakes and pigments in their powder form, prior to incorporation with binders and fillers and so on, offered the opportunity to examine the inorganic and organic constituents by spectroscopic and chromatographic methods in conjunction with historically available texts. raman spectroscopy and hplc-dad (and hplc-ms) permitted the identification of plant and insect anthraquinones (madder with varying compositions of alizarin, purpurin and pseudopurpurin as highlighted by sers), carminic acid and possibly acid stable carmine. a combination of traditional (alum and kaolin) and modern inorganic substrates (metallic salts of fe, sn, cu, pb and zn and barium sulfate) was ascertained by means of x-ray fluorescence and mid-ftir, while raman provided the information regarding the possible complexation of these pigments in the form of lakes. furthermore, raman can distinguish mixtures with the newer synthetic azo pigments (acid red 73, acid red 9/acid brown 6) and possibly xanthene dyes with numerous metallic salts and barium sulfate, drawing an overview of organic laboratory artist pigment preparations from the end of 19th century to the start of the 20th century. micro-raman spectroscopy analysis of a set of materials belonging to the iberian culture, dated between the sixth and the third century bc, was performed by tu n et al.20 on objects located in various archaeological sites of the spanish provinces of ja n, granada, malaga and ciudad real (spain), with the aim to clarify the processes of manufacturing and decoration of various kinds of materials, as well as the use of particular raw materials, including pigments.. the typology of these materials included ceramics and coverings with and without decoration. gypsum was detected as the main raw material used for the inside coverings of houses and tombs, as well as for storage structures, while calcite, dolomite and quartz were less used. as to decoration in ceramics, the origin and elaboration of black decoration are here identified for the first time in the history of iberian culture. black decoration can be classified as two periods: the older period used manganese oxide and the later period used magnetite. cinnabar has also been identified in the red decoration of ceramics retrieved as grave goods. raman spectroscopy combined with synchrotron radiation-based techniques and electron microprobe was used by wang et al.21 to study the yellow component of slips of marbled sigillata from 43 shreds. the elemental survey performed by electron microprobe analysis emphasized that the yellow component was made from a titanium-rich clay preparation while x-ray absorption near edge structure investigation at ti k-edge confirmed the massive presence of pseudobrookite (fe2tio5). raman spectroscopy was correlated with x-ray absorption near edge structure results in order to extract the raman spectra of pseudobrookite from these terra sigillata slips, which showed some differences with regard to the pure fe2tio5 pseudobrookite mineral phase. muda-trzebiatowska et al.22 reported the results of the surface layer study performed by means of the raman and complementary spectroscopic techniques for a collection of medieval copper objects, which remained submerged in sea water at a depth of 16 m as cargo part of the ship which sunk in 1408 in gda sk bay. the investigated collection consists of ca 230 ingots of copper. the surface porosity and encrustation coverage of the excavated ingots indicate that the original dimensions and masses were larger and decreased because of long-term exposure to corrosive and biologically active saline environment. in the raman spectra of superficial layers, the presence of bands corresponding to atacamite (cu2(oh)3cl), chalcopyrite (cufes2) and cuprite (cu2o) was observed together with a band centred at 1473 cm 1 ascribed to the organic oxammite [(nh4)2(c2o4) h2o] compound. all these degradation compounds appear as a consequence of the years of ingots inmersed in sea water (chlorides) with a great biological activity (sulfur and oxalate compounds). barone et al.23 studied a set of 16 interesting red gems from a private collection by using a micro-raman laboratory apparatus equipped with different excitation sources. authors identified gems in terms of composition, in order to discriminate corundum, rubies (a red transparent gem variety of corundum, al2o3) and simulants. of the analysed gems, authors recognized five simulants (two garnets, one rubellite, one glass, one doublet) and 11 rubies. the obtained results allow not only discriminating rubies from simulant and fakes but also achieving useful information on inclusions and treatments, obtaining a complete characterization of the studied red gems. the results on the studied gems once again epifanio juli n garay caicedo, 1796 1883) belonging to the collection of the national museum of colombia. the aim was not only to characterize the artistic materials but also to understand the transition from colonial times in the use of materials and the change of the oil on canvas technique in the country during the xixth century where colombia became open to global arts as well as techniques, styles and possibilities of representation apart from religious situations. this time coincided with the introduction of industrialization and the development of commercial and portable painting materials, resulting in the creation of a formal art academy in colombia. a novel method for handling and storing samples obtained by micro cut was developed, which allowed direct
